chapter: Style, the future of jazz and later playing
title: Updating old arrangements through phrasing
summary: Old arrangements can sound modern or period depending on the phrasing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What do you think about taking music like that, that was written in the ’30s and arranged in the ’30s – how do you as a musician approach music that you heard in its original form but are playing today in 1992? What’s your own approach?

There are different types of phrasings. You try to play – you can play – they’re the same notes, but you can just change the phrasing so that it sounds more modern than what it did in those days. I wish I could think of an example. Say [Wilder sings a brief phrase] something like that. In the old days, they might have played [he sings it again]. They’d play like that. In the phrasing today, they would try it smoothly, play a little more smoothly [he sings it with one note flowing into the next] or something like that, and it sounds more modern, in keeping with the way they play today, and yet it’s the same song and the same notes. That’s what the difference is. Sometimes you want it to sound like the ’20s. In fact, when we do the Garrison Keillor show, we’re playing music from that era, and we play just the way they played in those days. If you listen to it, you say, Jeez, there’s a band from the ’20s or the ’30s. But you could also take that same music and change the phrasing, and it would sound more modern.
So really it’s the phrasing that gives it the era.
It is, yeah. It’s a concept.
